**The Weight of a Single Word**

There’s a moment, just before dawn, when the world holds its breath. The air is thick with the kind of silence that isn’t absence but presence—like the pause between heartbeats, the space where something unspoken lingers. I’ve always been fascinated by these in-between places, the cracks in reality where meaning seeps through like water through stone. And if I had to name the thing that seeps, I’d call it *language*.

Words are strange, aren’t they? They’re the tools we use to carve out our existence, yet they’re also the very things that fail us when we need them most. A single word can be a lifeline or a noose, a bridge or a wall. *Love* is four letters, but it’s also the weight of a thousand unsaid things. *Sorry* is five, but it can feel like a stone in your mouth. And *goodbye*—well, *goodbye* is seven letters that might as well be seven knives.

I’ve spent years collecting words, hoarding them like a dragon with its gold. Not just the big, shiny ones—*serendipity*, *petrichor*, *sonder*—but the small, quiet ones too. The ones that don’t get invited to the party but show up anyway, unassuming and necessary. *Dust*. *Whisper*. *Almost*. *Enough*. These are the words that do the real work, the ones that hold up the sky when the fancy ones get tired.

There’s a word in Japanese—*komorebi*—that means the sunlight filtering through the leaves of trees. It’s a word that doesn’t exist in English, not really. We have *dappled light* or *sunbeams*, but those don’t quite capture it. *Komorebi* is specific. It’s a feeling as much as a sight. It’s the way the world looks when you’re lying on your back in the grass, half-asleep, half-awake, and the light moves across your eyelids like a slow, golden tide. English doesn’t have a word for that. And maybe that’s okay. Maybe some things are meant to be felt rather than named.

But then there are the words we *do* have, the ones that cut too deep. *Abandoned*. *Betrayal*. *Never*. These are the words that leave scars. I’ve said them. I’ve had them said to me. And in the saying, something shifts—irreversible, like a glass dropped on tile. You can sweep up the pieces, but the floor will never be the same.

I wonder sometimes if words are more powerful when they’re *not* said. The things we swallow, the things we let sit in our chests like stones. There’s a kind of magic in silence, in the way two people can sit together, not speaking, and still understand each other better than if they’d filled the air with noise. But then, there’s also the danger of silence—the way it can fester, the way it can become a habit, a prison. How do you know when to speak and when to stay quiet? How do you know which words will heal and which will wound?

I’ve been thinking a lot about names lately. Not just the ones we’re given, but the ones we choose for ourselves. Names are the first words we learn to recognize, the first sounds that mean *you*. And yet, so many of us spend our lives trying to outrun them. We change them, soften them, twist them into shapes that fit better. But no matter how many times you rename yourself, the old name lingers, like a ghost in the syllables.

There’s a story I read once about a man who lost his name. Not in the way you’d think—he didn’t forget it, or have it stolen. He just… stopped using it. He went years without hearing it spoken aloud, and one day, he realized he couldn’t remember what it sounded like. Not the way his mother said it when he was a child, not the way his lover whispered it in the dark. It was just… gone. And in its place was this hollow space, this absence where something essential had been. That’s the power of a name, I think. It’s not just a word. It’s a spell.

I’ve always been drawn to stories—books, myths, the kind of tales people tell when they think no one’s listening. Stories are how we make sense of the chaos. They’re the words we use to stitch the world back together when it falls apart. But here’s the thing about stories: they’re never just one thing. The same tale can be a warning or a comfort, depending on who’s telling it. *Little Red Riding Hood* is a story about danger, but it’s also a story about growing up. *The Odyssey* is about a man trying to get home, but it’s also about what happens when you spend too long looking backward.

I used to think that if I could just find the right words, I could explain everything—the way my heart races when I see the ocean, the way some songs make my ribs ache, the way grief sits in my throat like a swallowed coin. But now I’m not so sure. Maybe some things can’t be put into words. Maybe that’s why we have music, why we have art, why we have silence. Maybe the things that matter most are the things we can’t name.

Still, I keep trying. I keep writing, keep stringing words together like beads on a thread, hoping that if I arrange them just right, they’ll add up to something true. And sometimes, they do. Not always. But sometimes.

There’s a line from a poem I love—*"Tell all the truth but tell it slant."* I think about that a lot. The truth is too bright, too sharp. It needs to be softened, angled, so it doesn’t blind us. That’s what words are for, I think. Not to capture the truth, but to point toward it, like a finger pointing at the moon. The finger isn’t the moon. But without it, we might never look up.

I don’t know if I’ve said anything useful here. I don’t even know if I’ve said anything *true*. But I’ve said something. And maybe that’s enough.

For now.
